extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and students of dramatic theory studying or composing tragic drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing tragedies (plot, character, recognition, spectacle, and performance) following Aristotle's Poetics: what makes a tragic plot effective and how to shape characters, incidents, and recognitions to produce pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity/singleness of plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A well constructed plot should, therefore, be single in its issue, rather than double.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer one main action/issue (not two competing threads). The text contrasts single tragic plots (e.g., Oedipus) with double-threaded plots (like the Odyssey) and argues single plots produce the proper tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of fortune (peripeteia) direction
rubrics_metrics.description: A change of fortune should be not from bad to good, but, reversely, from good to bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy requires a reversal that moves from a better state to a worse one to elicit tragic pity and fear; plots that move from bad to good give a different (non-tragic) pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation by error or frailty (hamartia), not vice
rubrics_metrics.description: It should come about as the result not of vice, but of some great error or frailty in a character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The protagonist's misfortune should arise from a mistake or human frailty rather than moral corruption; this makes the suffering tragic rather than merely deserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double/opposite catastrophes for true tragic pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is better when not like the Odyssey, which has a double thread of plot and opposite catastrophes for the good and the bad; such double plots yield pleasure of the spectators' weakness, not true tragic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If aiming for authentic tragic effect, avoid structuring the play around equal opposite outcomes for different strands/characters (i.e., paired good/bad catastrophes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose subjects with moving incidents (few houses/families)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best tragedies are founded on the story of a few houses,—on the fortunes of Alcmaeon, Oedipus, Orestes... They are compelled to have recourse to those houses whose history contains moving incidents like these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subjects where familial ties produce compelling situations (recognition, kin-slaying, etc.). This is why tragedy historically concentrates on a small number of families with dramatic histories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic effect should come from inner structure, not spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacular means; but they may also result from the inner structure of the piece, which is the better way, and indicates a superior poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to produce pity and fear via plot construction and incidents (imitation), not by relying on visual spectacle. Spectacle that produces only the monstrous is an inferior method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must produce pity/fear when heard (auditory effectiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot ought to be so constructed that, even without the aid of the eye, he who hears the tale told will thrill with horror and melt to pity at what takes place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design incidents and their causal logic so the narrative alone (recited) generates the intended emotions; avoid dependence on purely stage effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidents should occur between those who are near (kin/friends)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions capable of this effect must happen between persons who are either friends or enemies or indifferent to one another. ... But when the tragic incident occurs between those who are near or dear to one another ... these are the situations to be looked for by the poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer tragic deeds involving kinship or close relationships (brother killing brother, son his father, mother her son, etc.), because these relations intensify pity and horror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skilful handling of traditional material (invention within framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: He ought not indeed destroy the framework of the received legends ... but he ought to show invention of his own, and skilfully handle the traditional material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting myths/legends, retain recognizable framework but introduce original treatment and skillful manipulations of incidents to heighten tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of the horrific deed — preferred dramatic arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: There are ways the deed may occur: done with knowledge; done in ignorance and discovery afterwards; about to act with knowledge and then not act; about to act knowing the persons and then not to act is the worst. Of all these ways, to be about to act knowing the persons, and then not to act, is the worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rank of effectiveness: best — deed perpetrated in ignorance with discovery after (startling effect without shocking unfairness); worse — deed perpetrated knowingly; worst — 'about to act' with knowledge then abstain (shocking but not tragic). Use examples (Cresphontes, Iphigenia, Oedipus) to model the best arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character — goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: First, and most important, it must be good. ... The character will be good if the purpose is good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protagonists should be fundamentally good (so their fall arouses pity). Goodness is relative to class (e.g., a woman or slave can be 'good' within their social type).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character — propriety/fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: The second thing to aim at is propriety. There is a type of manly valour; but valour in a woman, or unscrupulous cleverness, is inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traits must suit the character's social role, sex, or station; avoid unsuited qualities that break audience plausibility (e.g., implausible masculine courage in a character where it is inappropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character — true to life (verisimilitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thirdly, character must be true to-life: for this is a distinct thing from goodness and propriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be believable and lifelike; even when ennobled, they must preserve recognizable human traits and motivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character — consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth point is consistency: for though the subject of the Imitation, who suggested the style, may be inconsistent, still he must be consistently inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain internal coherence—if a character behaves inconsistently, that inconsistency must itself be stable and intelligible; avoid motiveless degradations or abrupt changes with no cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions and unravelling must follow necessity or probability (causal coherence)
rubrics_metrics.description: As in the structure of the plot, so too in the portraiture of character, the poet should always aim either at the necessary or the probable. ... the unravelling, no less than the complication, must arise out of the plot itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure events follow by logical necessity or credible probability from prior actions/traits; avoid arbitrary or irrational turns in the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Deus ex Machina within the drama
rubrics_metrics.description: It must not be brought about by the aid Deus ex Machina... The Deus ex Machina should be employed only for events external to the drama—for antecedent or subsequent events which lie beyond the range of human knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not resolve central plot problems by implausible external interventions; if used, restrict to matters outside the drama's temporal scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis) — prefer incident-driven recognitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all recognitions, the best is that which arises from the incidents themselves, where the startling discovery is made by natural means. ... These recognitions alone dispense with the artificial aid of tokens or amulets. Next come the recognitions by process of reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design recognitions that flow naturally from plot incidents (e.g., Oedipus), then reasoning-based recognitions; avoid artificial or poet-invented devices that feel contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition — taxonomy and ranking of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Kinds of recognition: (1) by signs/tokens (congenital or acquired scars, necklaces); (2) by a turn of incident (e.g., the Bath Scene in the Odyssey); (3) invented at will by the poet (nearly allied to fault); (4) by memory (sight or sound awakens feeling); (5) by process of reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tokens/formal proofs are less artistic; poet-invented verbal revelations are faulty; aim for higher-ranked types (incident-driven, memory, reasoning) for artistry and naturalness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the scene vividly (stage visualization to avoid inconsistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet—should place the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes—In this way, seeing everything with the utmost vividness, as if he were a spectator of the action, he will discover what is in keeping with it, and be most unlikely to overlook inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualize stage geography, sight lines, and movements during composition to prevent stage oversights (example: the failure of Carcinus where Amphiaraus' movement was neglected).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate gestures and naturalistic acting
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should work out his play, to the best of his power, with appropriate gestures; for those who feel emotion are most convincing through natural sympathy with the characters they represent; one who is agitated storms, one who is angry rages, with the most life-like reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan actor behaviour/gestures so that emotion is authentic and produces natural sympathy; performance details matter to the play's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story construction: outline then episodes; episodes must be relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: He should first sketch its general outline, and then fill in the episodes and amplify in detail. ... After this, the names being once given, it remains to fill in the episodes. We must see that they are relevant to the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a compact general plan, then add episodes that serve the main action; keep episodes short and pertinent (avoid extraneous material that belongs to epic extension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Complication and Unravelling; master both knot and unravelling
rubrics_metrics.description: By the Complication I mean all that extends from the beginning of the action and the part which marks the turning-point to good or bad fortune. The Unravelling is that which extends from the beginning of the change to the end. In speaking of a tragedy as the same or different, the best test to take is the plot. Identity exists where the Complication and Unravelling are the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully construct the progression from complication to unravelling so the plot is coherent and unified; many poets tie the knot well but unravel it ill—both arts must be mastered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to combine the greatest number of important poetic merits
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should endeavour if possible, to combine all poetic merits; or—failing that—the greatest number and those the most important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance virtues (plot complexity, recognition, reversal, character, diction, spectacle as appropriate) and prioritize major qualities rather than excelling in only one line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and ennoble types (represent persons above common level)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since Tragedy is an imitation of persons who are above the common level, the example of good portrait-painters should be followed. They ... make a likeness which is true to life and yet more beautiful. So too the poet ... should preserve the type—and yet ennoble it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing elevated or exceptional characters, keep likeness to real human traits but idealize them artistically (e.g., Achilles' portrayal).
